claim: Mammalian sirtuin 6 (Sirt6) is a conserved NAD+-dependent deacylase and mono-ADP ribosylase.
source: Mammalian sirtuin 6 (Sirt6) is a conserved NAD+-dependent deacylase and mono-ADP ribosylase that is known to be involved in DNA damage repair, metabolic homeostasis, inflammation, tumorigenesis, and aging.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SIRT6's enzymatic activities.

claim: Sirt6 is involved in DNA damage repair, metabolic homeostasis, inflammation, tumorigenesis, and aging.
source: Mammalian sirtuin 6 (Sirt6) is a conserved NAD+-dependent deacylase and mono-ADP ribosylase that is known to be involved in DNA damage repair, metabolic homeostasis, inflammation, tumorigenesis, and aging.
evidence: This statement references known roles of SIRT6 from existing literature.

claim: Loss of Sirt6 in mice results in accelerated aging and premature death within a month.
source: Loss of Sirt6 in mice results in accelerated aging and premature death within a month.
evidence: This is a well-established finding from prior research on Sirt6-deficient mice.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 dramatically extends the lifespan of both female and male Sirt6-deficient mice.
source: Here, we show that haploinsufficiency (i.e., heterozygous deletion) of Trp53 dramatically extends the lifespan of both female and male Sirt6-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by survival data presented in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues reduced body size and weight.
source: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues several age-related phenotypes of Sirt6-deficient mice, including reduced body size and weight, lordokyphosis, colitis, premature senescence, apoptosis, and bone marrow stem cell decline.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2A-C showing body size and weight measurements.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues lordokyphosis.
source: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues several age-related phenotypes of Sirt6-deficient mice, including reduced body size and weight, lordokyphosis, colitis, premature senescence, apoptosis, and bone marrow stem cell decline.
evidence: This is supported by X-ray imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues colitis.
source: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues several age-related phenotypes of Sirt6-deficient mice, including reduced body size and weight, lordokyphosis, colitis, premature senescence, apoptosis, and bone marrow stem cell decline.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues premature senescence.
source: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues several age-related phenotypes of Sirt6-deficient mice, including reduced body size and weight, lordokyphosis, colitis, premature senescence, apoptosis, and bone marrow stem cell decline.
evidence: This is supported by senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining data in Figure 1B-C and Figure 3D.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues apoptosis.
source: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues several age-related phenotypes of Sirt6-deficient mice, including reduced body size and weight, lordokyphosis, colitis, premature senescence, apoptosis, and bone marrow stem cell decline.
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues bone marrow stem cell decline.
source: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 in Sirt6-deficient mice rescues several age-related phenotypes of Sirt6-deficient mice, including reduced body size and weight, lordokyphosis, colitis, premature senescence, apoptosis, and bone marrow stem cell decline.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data on stem cell populations shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: SIRT6 deacetylates p53 at lysine 381.
source: Mechanistically, SIRT6 deacetylates p53 at lysine 381 to negatively regulate the stability and activity of p53.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro deacetylation assays shown in Figure 5E-F and immunofluorescence data in Figure 5H-J.

claim: SIRT6 deacetylation of p53 at lysine 381 negatively regulates the stability of p53.
source: Mechanistically, SIRT6 deacetylates p53 at lysine 381 to negatively regulate the stability and activity of p53.
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: SIRT6 deacetylation of p53 at lysine 381 negatively regulates the activity of p53.
source: Mechanistically, SIRT6 deacetylates p53 at lysine 381 to negatively regulate the stability and activity of p53.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced expression of p53 target genes in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 1F-G).

claim: Elevated p53 activity contributes significantly to accelerated aging in Sirt6-deficient mice.
source: These findings establish that elevated p53 activity contributes significantly to accelerated aging in Sirt6-deficient mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the dramatic rescue of aging phenotypes and lifespan extension when p53 is reduced by haploinsufficiency.

claim: p53 is a substrate of SIRT6.
source: Our study demonstrates that p53 is a substrate of SIRT6, and highlights the importance of SIRT6-p53 axis in the regulation of aging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 5A-B) and deacetylation assays (Figure 5C-F).

claim: The SIRT6-p53 axis is important in the regulation of aging.
source: Our study demonstrates that p53 is a substrate of SIRT6, and highlights the importance of SIRT6-p53 axis in the regulation of aging.
evidence: This is supported by the dramatic lifespan extension and phenotype rescue observed when p53 is reduced in Sirt6-deficient mice.

claim: Mice deficient in Sirt6 exhibit severe premature aging phenotypes including metabolic defects, lymphopenia, osteoporosis, genomic instability, and early death by 4 weeks of age.
source: Mice deficient in Sirt6 exhibit severe premature aging phenotypes, including metabolic defects, lymphopenia, osteoporosis, genomic instability, and early death by 4 weeks of age (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006) describing Sirt6-deficient mouse phenotypes.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sirt6 extends the lifespan of male mice by 15%.
source: Additionally, the ectopic expression of Sirt6 has been shown to extend the lifespan of male mice by 15% (Kanfi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication (Kanfi et al., 2012) showing lifespan extension by SIRT6 overexpression.

claim: Sirt6 deacetylates histone H3 at lysine 9 and 56 in a NAD+-dependent manner.
source: Sirt6 was first identified to deacetylate histone H3 at lysine 9 and 56 (in a NAD+-dependent manner) at the telomeres, promoter regions of target genes and globally as well, to mediate DNA damage repair, maintain telomeric metabolism, suppress NF-κB pathway in promoting longevity and regulate cell cycle (Kawahara et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2008; Michishita et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement cites multiple publications describing SIRT6's histone deacetylase activity.

claim: Sirt6 mediates DNA damage repair through its NAD+-dependent deacetylating activity.
source: The intricate roles of Sirt6 in DNA damage repair and metabolic regulation have been reported to stem from its inherent NAD+-dependent deacetylating activity on histones, CtIP, GCN5 and others, apart from its NAD+-dependent mono-ADP ribosylase activity (Dominy et al., 2012; Kaidi et al., 2010; Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites publications describing SIRT6's role in DNA damage repair through deacetylation.

claim: Sirt6 regulates metabolic processes through its NAD+-dependent deacetylating activity on histones, CtIP, GCN5 and others.
source: The intricate roles of Sirt6 in DNA damage repair and metabolic regulation have been reported to stem from its inherent NAD+-dependent deacetylating activity on histones, CtIP, GCN5 and others, apart from its NAD+-dependent mono-ADP ribosylase activity (Dominy et al., 2012; Kaidi et al., 2010; Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement cites publications describing SIRT6's metabolic regulatory functions.

claim: Sirt6-mediated regulation has been reported for NF-κB, AKT, and IGF1 signaling pathways.
source: Although Sirt6-mediated regulation has been reported for several signaling pathways (for example, NF-κB, AKT, and IGF1) (Kanfi et al., 2012; Kawahara et al., 2009; Pan et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2010), the key mechanism underlying the severe acceleration of aging and premature death in Sirt6-deficient mice remains elusive.
evidence: This statement cites multiple publications describing SIRT6's regulation of various signaling pathways.

claim: p53 is a tumor suppressor gene that triggers cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and/or senescence.
source: Trp53, also denoted as p53, is a tumor suppressor gene that triggers cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and/or senescence (Rufini et al., 2013; Vousden and Prives, 2009).
evidence: This statement cites publications describing p53's tumor suppressor functions.

claim: p53 has been widely implicated in premature senescence and aging.
source: p53 has been widely implicated in premature senescence and aging (Hinkal et al., 2009; Poyurovsky and Prives, 2010; Varela et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement cites publications linking p53 to senescence and aging.

claim: p53 was the first non-histone protein identified to undergo acetylation as a post-translational modification.
source: p53 was the first non-histone protein identified to undergo acetylation as a post-translational modification (Gu and Roeder, 1997).
evidence: This statement cites the original publication identifying p53 acetylation.

claim: Lysine 382 in the C-terminus of p53 undergoes marked acetylation followed by lysine 381 and 373.
source: Lysine 382, localized in the C-terminus of p53, is identified to undergo marked acetylation followed by lysine 381 and 373 (Gu and Roeder, 1997).
evidence: This statement cites a publication describing the major acetylation sites on p53.

claim: p53 has a half-life of around 30 minutes.
source: Given the stunted half-life of around 30 min for p53, these acetylations have been reported to impart stability to p53, which then mediates a range of downstream functions in response to DNA damage, oncogenic stress, age-associated abnormalities, tumor suppression and others (Donehower, 2009; Lozano, 2010; Vousden and Prives, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about p53 protein stability.

claim: Acetylations of p53 impart stability to p53.
source: Given the stunted half-life of around 30 min for p53, these acetylations have been reported to impart stability to p53, which then mediates a range of downstream functions in response to DNA damage, oncogenic stress, age-associated abnormalities, tumor suppression and others (Donehower, 2009; Lozano, 2010; Vousden and Prives, 2009).
evidence: This statement cites publications describing how acetylation stabilizes p53.

claim: In laminopathy-based progeria, mutant lamin A results in elevated p53 signaling.
source: In laminopathy-based progeria, mutant lamin A results in elevated p53 signaling and reducing p53 level significantly ameliorates premature aging phenotypes and extends lifespan (Varela et al., 2005), thus suggesting that activation of p53-dependent downstream signaling accelerates aging.
evidence: This statement cites a publication linking mutant lamin A to elevated p53 in progeria.

claim: Reducing p53 level significantly ameliorates premature aging phenotypes and extends lifespan in laminopathy-based progeria.
source: In laminopathy-based progeria, mutant lamin A results in elevated p53 signaling and reducing p53 level significantly ameliorates premature aging phenotypes and extends lifespan (Varela et al., 2005), thus suggesting that activation of p53-dependent downstream signaling accelerates aging.
evidence: This statement cites a publication showing rescue of progeria phenotypes by reducing p53.

claim: Activation of p53-dependent downstream signaling accelerates aging.
source: In laminopathy-based progeria, mutant lamin A results in elevated p53 signaling and reducing p53 level significantly ameliorates premature aging phenotypes and extends lifespan (Varela et al., 2005), thus suggesting that activation of p53-dependent downstream signaling accelerates aging.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reducing p53 ameliorates aging phenotypes in progeria.

claim: Lamin A is an endogenous activator of SIRT6.
source: Interestingly, lamin A is an endogenous activator of SIRT6 and mutant lamin A results in compromised SIRT6 deacetylase activity (Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement cites a publication showing lamin A activates SIRT6.

claim: Mutant lamin A results in compromised SIRT6 deacetylase activity.
source: Interestingly, lamin A is an endogenous activator of SIRT6 and mutant lamin A results in compromised SIRT6 deacetylase activity (Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement cites a publication showing mutant lamin A impairs SIRT6 activity.

claim: Downstream targets of p53, including p21, Puma, Noxa, Bax and Ddit4, were upregulated in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mouse embryonic fibroblasts compared to Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ MEFs.
source: Intriguingly, a range of downstream targets of p53, including p21, Puma, Noxa, Bax and Ddit4 (Poyurovsky and Prives, 2010), were upregulated in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) as compared to Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+MEFs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loss of Sirt6 results in premature senescence.
source: Consistent with previous reports stating that loss of Sirt6 results in premature senescence (Mao et al., 2012; Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs exhibited enhanced senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity and senescence-like flattened cellular morphology at passage 6 (P6) (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining data in Figure 1B-C and morphology images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs exhibited enhanced senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity at passage 6.
source: Consistent with previous reports stating that loss of Sirt6 results in premature senescence (Mao et al., 2012; Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs exhibited enhanced senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity and senescence-like flattened cellular morphology at passage 6 (P6) (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs exhibited senescence-like flattened cellular morphology at passage 6.
source: Consistent with previous reports stating that loss of Sirt6 results in premature senescence (Mao et al., 2012; Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs exhibited enhanced senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity and senescence-like flattened cellular morphology at passage 6 (P6) (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by morphology images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs exhibited enhanced p16 levels at P6.
source: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs also exhibited enhanced p16 levels at P6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly rescued the senescence-associated phenotypes in Sirt6-/- MEFs at P6.
source: However, haploinsufficiency of Trp53 significantly rescued the senescence-associated phenotypes in Sirt6-/- MEFs at P6 (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, 3 independent batches of MEFs have been used in the study which were obtained from independent batches of littermate embryos).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing reduced senescence markers.

claim: Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly attenuated p16 levels in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs.
source: Also, Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly attenuated p16 levels and the enhanced expression of the downstream targets of p53 in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly attenuated the enhanced expression of the downstream targets of p53 in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs.
source: Also, Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly attenuated p16 levels and the enhanced expression of the downstream targets of p53 in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Enhancement of sensitivity to DNA damage upon loss of Sirt6 has been previously reported.
source: Enhancement of sensitivity to DNA damage upon loss of Sirt6 has been previously reported (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication describing DNA damage sensitivity in Sirt6-deficient cells.

claim: The increased sensitivity to DNA damage in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs treated with gamma-irradiation was substantially attenuated in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs.
source: Again, the increased sensitivity to DNA damage in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs treated with gamma-irradiation was substantially attenuated in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by cell survival data after irradiation in Figure 1D and images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The decreased cell viability of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs was significantly improved in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs.
source: The decreased cell viability of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ MEFs was significantly improved in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- MEFs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown by MTT assay data in Figure 1E.

claim: There was a significant upregulation of the expression of several downstream targets of p53 in the liver, kidneys, and spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: Consistent with our findings in MEFs (Figure 1A), there was a significant upregulation of the expression of several downstream targets of p53 in the liver, kidneys, and spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 1F and G and Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 1F-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly suppressed the expression of downstream targets of p53 in the liver, kidneys, and spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice.
source: However, Trp53 haploinsufficiency significantly suppressed the expression of those downstream targets of p53 in the liver, kidneys, and spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice (Figure 1F and G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 1F-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The upregulation of p53 targets upon loss of Sirt6 is a consequence of p53 activation.
source: This further suggests that the upregulation of these targets upon loss of Sirt6 is indeed a consequence of p53 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reducing p53 levels suppresses these targets.

claim: Majority of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice exhibited severe premature aging and were much smaller than their wild-type littermates at 3 weeks of age.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), majority of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice exhibited severe premature aging and were much smaller than their wild-type littermates at 3 weeks of age (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by images in Figure 2A and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice appeared much healthier than the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates post 3 weeks of birth.
source: Interestingly, the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice appeared much healthier than the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates post 3 weeks of birth (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by images in Figure 2A.

claim: Both female and male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were significantly larger in body size than their Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates.
source: Though smaller than their littermate wild-type (Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+) controls, both female and male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were significantly larger in body size than their Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 2A n=25-35 for all three genotypes).
evidence: This is shown by images in Figure 2A with sample sizes of n=25-35.

claim: The mean body weights of both female and male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were significantly more than that of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates.
source: The mean body weights of both female and male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were also significantly more than that of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown by body weight data in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice exhibited a 16-fold increase in maximum lifespan compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: The Sirt6-deficient mice mostly died within 4 weeks of birth, whereas the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- littermate mice exhibited striking extensions in lifespan: female mice exhibited a 16-fold increase in maximum lifespan and 11-fold increase in median lifespan (Figure 2D); males showed a 14-fold extension in maximum lifespan and a 7.5-fold extension in median lifespan (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2D.

claim: Female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice exhibited an 11-fold increase in median lifespan compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: The Sirt6-deficient mice mostly died within 4 weeks of birth, whereas the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- littermate mice exhibited striking extensions in lifespan: female mice exhibited a 16-fold increase in maximum lifespan and 11-fold increase in median lifespan (Figure 2D); males showed a 14-fold extension in maximum lifespan and a 7.5-fold extension in median lifespan (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2D.

claim: Male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice showed a 14-fold extension in maximum lifespan compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: The Sirt6-deficient mice mostly died within 4 weeks of birth, whereas the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- littermate mice exhibited striking extensions in lifespan: female mice exhibited a 16-fold increase in maximum lifespan and 11-fold increase in median lifespan (Figure 2D); males showed a 14-fold extension in maximum lifespan and a 7.5-fold extension in median lifespan (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2E.

claim: Male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice showed a 7.5-fold extension in median lifespan compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: The Sirt6-deficient mice mostly died within 4 weeks of birth, whereas the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- littermate mice exhibited striking extensions in lifespan: female mice exhibited a 16-fold increase in maximum lifespan and 11-fold increase in median lifespan (Figure 2D); males showed a 14-fold extension in maximum lifespan and a 7.5-fold extension in median lifespan (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2E.

claim: Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice had median lifespan of 56–64 weeks.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Jacks et al., 1994; Tyner et al., 2002), we found that Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice had median lifespan of 56–64 weeks (Figure 2D and E), and mostly succumbed to tumors by 72–80 weeks.
evidence: This is shown by survival curves in Figure 2D-E and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice mostly succumbed to tumors by 72–80 weeks.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Jacks et al., 1994; Tyner et al., 2002), we found that Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice had median lifespan of 56–64 weeks (Figure 2D and E), and mostly succumbed to tumors by 72–80 weeks.
evidence: This is consistent with previous reports on p53 heterozygous mice.

claim: At four weeks of age, the Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice exhibited no significant differences from Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ mice in either body size or body weight.
source: However, at four weeks of age, the Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice exhibited no significant differences from Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ (wild-type) mice in either body size or body weight.
evidence: This is an observation from the study comparing p53 heterozygous mice to wild-type at 4 weeks.

claim: The body weights of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice increased steadily with age as did their wild-type littermates, although they always weighed less than their WT littermate mice.
source: The body weights of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice (both females and males) increased steadily with age as did their wild-type (WT) littermates, although they always weighed less than their WT littermate mice (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is shown by body weight tracking data in Figure 2F-G.

claim: At 3 weeks of age, the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were more active than the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice but were less active than their WT littermates.
source: At 3 weeks of age, the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were more active than the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+mice but were less active than their WT littermates.
evidence: This is an observational finding from the study.

claim: p53 protein level in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was decreased compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice, but was more than that of Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ mice.
source: While comparing p53 expression levels in the cells and tissues of 3-week old mice, p53 protein level in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was observed to be decreased as compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice, but was more than that of Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The serum IGF1 levels were drastically reduced in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice compared to Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ mice at the age of around 24 days.
source: As previously reported (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), the serum IGF1 levels were drastically reduced in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice as compared to Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ mice at the age of around 24 days .
evidence: This is consistent with previous reports and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The serum IGF1 levels in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were significantly rescued with respect to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice, but were less than that of their wild-type littermates.
source: Interestingly, the serum IGF1 levels in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were significantly rescued with respect to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice, but were less than that of their wild-type littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by serum IGF1 measurement data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The serum IGF1 levels of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were less than that of their wild-type littermates during their terminal stage (10-16 months).
source: Also, the serum IGF1 levels of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were less than that of their wild-type littermates during their terminal stage (10-16 months) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by serum IGF1 measurement data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice displayed a minor drop in their serum glucose levels.
source: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice displayed a minor drop in their serum glucose levels, while the compound mutant (Sirt6-/-Trp53+/-) mice exhibited an almost comparable glucose level to their wild-type littermates at the age of 24 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by serum glucose measurement data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The compound mutant (Sirt6-/-Trp53+/-) mice exhibited an almost comparable glucose level to their wild-type littermates at the age of 24 days.
source: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice displayed a minor drop in their serum glucose levels, while the compound mutant (Sirt6-/-Trp53+/-) mice exhibited an almost comparable glucose level to their wild-type littermates at the age of 24 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by serum glucose measurement data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice, in their terminal lifespan, had slightly reduced serum glucose levels than their wild-type littermates, but the values did not reach significance.
source: Although Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice, in their terminal lifespan, had slightly reduced serum glucose levels than their wild-type littermates, the values did not reach significance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by serum glucose measurement data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At around 24 days of age, the sizes of the internal organs of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice were markedly larger than those of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice, although they were smaller than those of wild-type littermates.
source: As expected, at around 24 days of age, the sizes of the internal organs of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice, such as spleen, thymus, kidney, liver, lungs and heart, were markedly larger than those of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice, although they were smaller than those of wild-type (Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+) littermates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by images of internal organs in Figure 3A.

claim: Lordokyphosis was significantly improved in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice, irrespective of gender.
source: Lordokyphosis (increased curvature of the spine), a prominent phenotype of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), was significantly improved in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/-mice, irrespective of gender (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by X-ray images in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Colitis was largely rescued in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice when compared to the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates.
source: Colitis, a characteristic feature previously reported in Sirt6-deficient mice (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006), was largely rescued in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice when compared to the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown by histological images in Figure 3C.

claim: There was significantly less senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity in the organs from Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: When senescence was evaluated, there was significantly less senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity in the organs from Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice, such as spleen, liver and kidneys, as compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 3D), thus suggesting a marked rescue of premature senescence in the compound mutant mice upon haploinsufficiency of Trp53.
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining images in Figure 3D.

claim: Approximately 26–28% of Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice developed tumors by 17–20 months, regardless of gender.
source: Approximately 26–28% of Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice developed tumors by 17–20 months, regardless of gender as already reported (Jacks et al., 1994; Tyner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is consistent with previous reports on p53 heterozygous mice.

claim: Around 32% of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice developed tumors during their terminal lifespan.
source: Interestingly, around 32% of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- (compound mutant) mice developed tumors during their terminal lifespan.
evidence: This is an observation from the study on tumor incidence in compound mutant mice.

claim: The incidence of cancer in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was earlier (9-16 months) than the Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice (17-20 months).
source: However, the incidence of cancer in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was earlier (9-16 months) than the Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice (17-20 months).
evidence: This is an observation from the study comparing tumor onset between genotypes.

claim: The Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice mostly developed sarcoma by 17-20 months.
source: The Sirt6+/+Trp53+/- mice mostly developed sarcoma by 17-20 months (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by tumor images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice developed kidney tumor (19%), prostate tumor (17%), bladder tumor (16%), and pancreatic tumor (8%).
source: However, the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice developed other types of tumors, such as kidney tumor (19%), prostate tumor (17%), bladder tumor (16%), and pancreatic tumor (8%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F respectively), while only 3% of them exhibited incidence of sarcoma.
evidence: This is shown by tumor images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F and represents tumor incidence data.

claim: Only 3% of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice exhibited incidence of sarcoma.
source: However, the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice developed other types of tumors, such as kidney tumor (19%), prostate tumor (17%), bladder tumor (16%), and pancreatic tumor (8%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F respectively), while only 3% of them exhibited incidence of sarcoma.
evidence: This is tumor incidence data from the study.

claim: Sirt6 depletion enhanced the onset and diversified the type of tumors in the Trp53+/- background.
source: Taken together, sirt6 depletion enhanced the onset and diversified the type of tumors in the Trp53+/- background, given that Sirt6 is a tumor suppressor itself (Lerrer and Cohen, 2013; Sebastián et al., 2012 ).
evidence: This is inferred from the earlier tumor onset and different tumor types in compound mutant mice, and cites SIRT6's tumor suppressor role.

claim: Some female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice succumbed to the disorder of incontinence at around 14-16 months.
source: Apart from severe body wasting and loss of vigour in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice in their terminal stage, some female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice succumbed to the disorder of incontinence at around 14-16 months, while around 95% of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- male mice exhibited penile protrusion at around 9-11 months of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from the study on late-life phenotypes.

claim: Around 95% of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- male mice exhibited penile protrusion at around 9-11 months of age.
source: Apart from severe body wasting and loss of vigour in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice in their terminal stage, some female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice succumbed to the disorder of incontinence at around 14-16 months, while around 95% of the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- male mice exhibited penile protrusion at around 9-11 months of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice remained sterile throughout their lifespan.
source: Also, the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice remained sterile throughout their lifespan.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Stem cell depletion is one of the hallmarks of premature aging.
source: Stem cell depletion is one of the hallmarks of premature aging and heterozygosity of Trp53 has been reported to improve stem cell maintenance (Amir et al., 2017; Belle et al., 2015; López-Otín et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about aging hallmarks, citing relevant literature.

claim: Heterozygosity of Trp53 has been reported to improve stem cell maintenance.
source: Stem cell depletion is one of the hallmarks of premature aging and heterozygosity of Trp53 has been reported to improve stem cell maintenance (Amir et al., 2017; Belle et al., 2015; López-Otín et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement cites publications showing p53 heterozygosity improves stem cell maintenance.

claim: There was a notable drop in the number of mesenchymal and hematopoietic stem cells derived from the bone marrow of both male and female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: Consistent with the age-associated decline of bone marrow stem cells, we observed a notable drop in the number of mesenchymal and hematopoietic stem cells derived from the bone marrow of both male and female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Upon Trp53 haploinsufficiency, the percentage of mesenchymal and hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was partially, yet significantly restored compared to their littermate Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: However, upon Trp53 haploinsufficiency, the percentage of mesenchymal and hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice (both females and males) was partially, yet significantly restored as compared to their littermate Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells undergo drastic reduction in the thymus of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice post 3 weeks of birth.
source: It has been previously reported that CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells undergo drastic reduction in the thymus of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+mice post 3 weeks of birth (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication describing thymic cell populations in Sirt6-deficient mice.

claim: There was a marked decline in the thymic CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice at around 24 days of age.
source: Consistently, we also observed a marked decline in the thymic CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice at around 24 days of age (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E-F.

claim: There was a striking increase in the number of CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells in the thymus of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice compared to that in the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates.
source: However, there was a striking increase in the number of CD4+CD8+ double-positive cells in the thymus of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice as compared to that in the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Apoptotic responses are upregulated in the thymus of Sirt6-deficient mice.
source: We confirmed the previous observation that apoptotic responses are upregulated in the thymus of Sirt6-deficient mice (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown by Annexin V staining data in Figure 4G and cites a previous publication.

claim: Apoptosis was partially rescued in both thymus and bone marrow stromal cells of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice when compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice.
source: Interestingly, this was partially rescued in both thymus and bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice when compared to Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is shown by Annexin V staining data in Figure 4G-H.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of B220+ cells in the spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice than that in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates.
source: In addition, there was a significant increase in the number of B220+ cells (characterizing B cells across all developmental stages) and CD11b+ cells (representing monocytes) in the spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice than that in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 4I and J), thus indicating that haploinsufficiency of Trp53 rescues the total B cell count and the total monocyte count, respectively, in Sirt6-deficient scenario.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4I.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of CD11b+ cells in the spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice than that in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates.
source: In addition, there was a significant increase in the number of B220+ cells (characterizing B cells across all developmental stages) and CD11b+ cells (representing monocytes) in the spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice than that in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 4I and J), thus indicating that haploinsufficiency of Trp53 rescues the total B cell count and the total monocyte count, respectively, in Sirt6-deficient scenario.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4J.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 rescues the total B cell count in Sirt6-deficient scenario.
source: In addition, there was a significant increase in the number of B220+ cells (characterizing B cells across all developmental stages) and CD11b+ cells (representing monocytes) in the spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice than that in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 4I and J), thus indicating that haploinsufficiency of Trp53 rescues the total B cell count and the total monocyte count, respectively, in Sirt6-deficient scenario.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased B220+ cells in compound mutant mice.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Trp53 rescues the total monocyte count in Sirt6-deficient scenario.
source: In addition, there was a significant increase in the number of B220+ cells (characterizing B cells across all developmental stages) and CD11b+ cells (representing monocytes) in the spleen of Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice than that in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ littermates (Figure 4I and J), thus indicating that haploinsufficiency of Trp53 rescues the total B cell count and the total monocyte count, respectively, in Sirt6-deficient scenario.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased CD11b+ cells in compound mutant mice.

claim: SIRT6 and p53 physically interact at the endogenous level.
source: Via co-immunoprecipitation with specific antibodies against SIRT6 and p53, we observed interaction between the two proteins at the endogenous level (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A.

claim: p53 can pull down SIRT6 in vitro, suggesting a direct interaction between SIRT6 and p53.
source: Indeed, p53 could pull down SIRT6 in vitro, suggesting a direct interaction between SIRT6 and p53 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro binding assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: A previous study has indicated that SIRT6, as a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, is not responsible for p53 deacetylation at lysine 382.
source: A previous study has indicated that SIRT6, as a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, is not responsible for p53 deacetylation at lysine (K) 382 (Michishita et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication showing SIRT6 does not deacetylate p53 at K382.

claim: SIRT6 can deacetylate p53 in vitro.
source: As predicted, we observed that SIRT6 could deacetylate p53 in vitro (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro deacetylation assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: SIRT6-mediated p53 deacetylation in vitro was abrogated in the absence of NAD+.
source: In line with the nature of SIRT6 as a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, SIRT6-mediated p53 deacetylation in vitro was abrogated in the absence of NAD+ (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro deacetylation assay data in Figure 5C-D.

claim: SIRT6-mediated p53 deacetylation was largely diminished in the presence of the sirtuin inhibitor nicotinamide.
source: In addition, this deacetylation was largely diminished in the presence of the sirtuin inhibitor nicotinamide (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro deacetylation assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: No alteration in p53 acetylation at lysine 382 was observed even with increasing concentration of rhSIRT6 in vitro.
source: In accordance with existing literature (Michishita et al., 2005), we observed no alteration in p53 acetylation at lysine (K) 382 even with increasing concentration of rhSIRT6 in vitro (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro deacetylation assay data in Figure 5E and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: The pan-acetylation and acetylation at K381 of p53 significantly reduced with increasing concentrations of SIRT6.
source: However, when checking the other two major sites of acetylation in the C-terminus of p53, that is lysine 381 and 373 (Gu and Roeder, 1997), the pan-acetylation (i.e., total acetylation) and acetylation at K381 of p53 was found to significantly reduce with increasing concentrations of SIRT6 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro deacetylation assay data in Figure 5E-F.

claim: No significant change in the acetylation of p53 at K373 was observed in the presence of rhSIRT6.
source: No significant change in the acetylation of p53 at K373 was observed in the presence of rhSIRT6 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is shown by in vitro deacetylation assay data in Figure 5E-F.

claim: p53 acetylation at K381 was upregulated in SIRT6-deficient cells in comparison with mock CRISPR control cells.
source: Consistently, p53 acetylation at K381 was upregulated in SIRT6-deficient cells (SIRT6 KO cells) in comparison with mock CRISPR control cells, when assessed with western blotting (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5G.

claim: No significant change in p53 acetylation at K382 was observed in SIRT6-deficient cells when compared with mock CRISPR control cells.
source: Again, no significant change in p53 acetylation at K382 was observed in SIRT6-deficient cells when compared with mock CRISPR control cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5G.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining showed that p53 acetylation was upregulated at K381, but not K382 in SIRT6-deficient cells.
source: In agreement with Western blotting results, immunofluorescence staining also showed that p53 acetylation was upregulated at K381, but not K382 in SIRT6-deficient cells (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence images in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Expression of the FLAG-tagged wild-type form of SIRT6 attenuated the upregulated p53 K381 acetylation in SIRT6-deficient HEK293 cells.
source: Additionally, expression of the FLAG-tagged wild-type (WT) form of SIRT6 attenuated the upregulated p53 K381 acetylation in SIRT6-deficient HEK293 cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence images in Figure 5I.

claim: Attenuation in p53 acetylation at K381 was not observed with the ectopic expression of the catalytically inactive form of SIRT6 (H133Y).
source: However, such attenuation in p53 acetylation at K381 was not observed with the ectopic expression of the catalytically inactive form of SIRT6 (H133Y) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence images in Figure 5J.

claim: Ectopically expressed SIRT6 (both active and catalytically inactive forms) had no effect on p53 acetylation at K382.
source: Although 90–95% of the SIRT6 KO cells were stained with antibodies against p53 acetylated at K382, ectopically expressed SIRT6 (both active and catalytically inactive forms) had no effect on p53 acetylation at K382 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence images in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Pan-acetylation of WT p53 was increased in the SIRT6-deficient cells over control cells.
source: Consistent with data shown in Figure 5G, pan-acetylation of WT p53 was increased in the SIRT6-deficient cells over control cells (Figure 5K and L) and the K381R mutation caused a significant reduction in pan-acetylation of p53 in both control and SIRT6-deficient cells (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5K-L.

claim: The K381R mutation caused a significant reduction in pan-acetylation of p53 in both control and SIRT6-deficient cells.
source: Consistent with data shown in Figure 5G, pan-acetylation of WT p53 was increased in the SIRT6-deficient cells over control cells (Figure 5K and L) and the K381R mutation caused a significant reduction in pan-acetylation of p53 in both control and SIRT6-deficient cells (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5K.

claim: The increase in pan-acetylation of p53 was largely diminished for K381R mutant in SIRT6-deficient cells compared to control cells.
source: Surprisingly, the increase in pan-acetylation of p53 was largely diminished for K381R mutant in SIRT6-deficient cells as compared to control cells (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5K-L.

claim: The increased p53 pan-acetylation in the absence of SIRT6 is largely attributable to the acetylation status at lysine 381 of p53.
source: These findings support the idea that the increased p53 pan-acetylation in the absence of SIRT6 is largely attributable to the acetylation status at lysine 381 of p53 (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: This is inferred from the K381R mutant data showing reduced pan-acetylation in Figure 5K-L.

claim: Endogenous p53 immunoprecipitated from SIRT6 KO HEK293 cells exhibited more acetylation at K381 compared to mock CRISPR cells.
source: Also, endogenous p53 immunoprecipitated from SIRT6 KO HEK293 cells exhibited more acetylation at K381 as compared to mock CRISPR cells, and this increased acetylation of p53 at K381 went down with ectopic expression of wild-type (WT) SIRT6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Increased acetylation of p53 at K381 in SIRT6 KO cells went down with ectopic expression of wild-type SIRT6.
source: Also, endogenous p53 immunoprecipitated from SIRT6 KO HEK293 cells exhibited more acetylation at K381 as compared to mock CRISPR cells, and this increased acetylation of p53 at K381 went down with ectopic expression of wild-type (WT) SIRT6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Upregulation of p53 acetylation at K381 was observed in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice compared to Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ littermate mice.
source: To further substantiate the observation of upregulation of p53 acetylation at K381 upon Sirt6 deficiency, we tested the same in cells and tissues of mice, and similarly observed upregulation of p53 acetylation at K381 in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice as compared to Sirt6+/+Trp53+/+ littermate mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I-J.

claim: Acetylation enhances the stability of p53.
source: It is known that acetylation enhances the stability of p53 (Gu and Zhu, 2012; Kruse and Gu, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about p53 regulation, citing relevant literature.

claim: HEK293 cells lacking SIRT6 had approximately two-fold increases in the total p53 protein level when compared with mock CRISPR control cells.
source: Indeed, HEK293 cells lacking SIRT6 (SIRT6 KO cells) had approximately two-fold increases in the total p53 protein level when compared with mock CRISPR control cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed the increased endogenous levels of p53 in SIRT6 KO cells compared to control cells.
source: Immunofluorescence staining further confirmed the increased endogenous levels of p53 in SIRT6 KO cells as compared to control cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence images in Figure 6C.

claim: Liver and kidney tissues from Sirt6-deficient mice exhibited a significant increase in p53 protein levels.
source: Similarly, liver and kidney tissues from Sirt6-deficient mice exhibited a significant increase in p53 protein levels (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Increase in p53 expression was observed in Sirt6 null primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: This increase in p53 expression was also observed in Sirt6 null (Sirt6-/-) primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts (passage P2 MEFs were used to avoid alterations because of serial passaging) (Figures Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot and immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide confirmed the enhanced stability of p53 in SIRT6-deficient cells.
source: Treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide further confirmed the enhanced stability of p53 in SIRT6-deficient cells (Figures Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown by cycloheximide chase experiment data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: No increased phosphorylation of p53 at serine 15 was observed in SIRT6-deficient HEK293 cells compared with wild-type cells without irradiation.
source: However, we did not observe increased phosphorylation of p53 at serine 15 in SIRT6-deficient HEK293 cells compared with wild-type cells without irradiation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 6F.

claim: Phosphorylation of p53 at serine 15 robustly increased in both wild type and Sirt6-deficient cells upon irradiation.
source: This phosphorylation of p53 robustly increased in both wild type and Sirt6-deficient cells upon irradiation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 6F.

claim: The upregulation of p53 in SIRT6-deficient cells is unlikely a direct consequence of increased DNA damage in the absence of SIRT6.
source: This suggests that the upregulation of p53 in SIRT6-deficient cells is unlikely a direct consequence of increased DNA damage in the absence of SIRT6 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increased p53 S15 phosphorylation without irradiation in Figure 6F.

claim: No significant increase in p53 mRNA levels was observed in the absence of Sirt6 in HEK293 cells, MEF cells or mice tissues.
source: Furthermore, we observed no significant increase in p53 mRNA levels in the absence of Sirt6 in HEK293 cells, MEF cells or mice tissues (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 6G-J.

claim: SIRT6 regulates p53 at the post-translational level.
source: Hence, it is likely that SIRT6 regulates p53 at the post-translational level.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased p53 protein levels without increased mRNA levels in SIRT6-deficient cells.

claim: p53 K381R mutant displayed a significant drop in stability.
source: As predicted, we observed a significant drop in the stability of p53 K381R mutant, which was further intensified upon cycloheximide treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown by cycloheximide chase experiment data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: p53 K381Q mutant displayed improved stability.
source: On the other hand, p53 K381Q mutant displayed improved stability, as evidenced by the comparable protein expression levels before and after cycloheximide treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown by cycloheximide chase experiment data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Loss of SIRT6 leads to upregulation of p53 acetylation at K381, which further confers stability to p53.
source: These findings reinstate that loss of SIRT6 leads to upregulation of p53 acetylation at K381, which further confers stability to p53.
evidence: This is inferred from the K381Q mutant showing improved stability and K381R showing reduced stability.

claim: Increase in the expression of senescent biomarker p16 was observed in SIRT6 KO cells with respect to control cells.
source: In agreement with increase in the expression of senescent biomarker p16 in SIRT6 KO cells with respect to control cells, we also observed an increase in the expression of p16 in cells with ectopic expression of p53 K381Q mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Increase in the expression of p16 was observed in cells with ectopic expression of p53 K381Q mutant.
source: In agreement with increase in the expression of senescent biomarker p16 in SIRT6 KO cells with respect to control cells, we also observed an increase in the expression of p16 in cells with ectopic expression of p53 K381Q mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Hyperacetylation of p53 at K381 imparts senescence-like properties to cells.
source: This data suggests that hyperacetylation of p53 at K381 imparts senescence-like properties to cells, thus contributing to the premature senescence observed in Sirt6-deficient cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased p16 expression in cells expressing p53 K381Q mutant.

claim: Recent studies have reported that p53 upregulates SIRT6 expression.
source: Although recent studies have reported that p53 upregulates SIRT6 expression (Jung et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014), the mechanistic explanation of this regulation remains largely unclear.
evidence: This statement cites publications showing p53 upregulates SIRT6.

claim: The mechanistic explanation of p53 upregulating SIRT6 expression remains largely unclear.
source: Although recent studies have reported that p53 upregulates SIRT6 expression (Jung et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014), the mechanistic explanation of this regulation remains largely unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There is no existing literature about the regulation of p53 by SIRT6.
source: On the other hand, there is no existing literature about the regulation of p53 by SIRT6.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of SIRT6 results in increased acetylation of p53, leading to elevated apoptosis and senescence at the cellular level and to accelerated aging in mice.
source: In this study, we show that loss of SIRT6 results in increased acetylation of p53, leading to elevated apoptosis and senescence at the cellular level and to accelerated aging in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings supported by multiple data figures.

claim: The study identified a novel SIRT6-p53 axis in the regulation of senescence and aging.
source: These data identified a novel SIRT6-p53 axis in the regulation of senescence and aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The stability of p53 is regulated through SIRT6-mediated deacetylation of p53 at K381.
source: Our study reveals a direct link between SIRT6 and p53, wherein the stability of p53 is regulated through SIRT6-mediated deacetylation of p53 at K381.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings on deacetylation and stability.

claim: SIRT6-mediated p53 deacetylation is a critical mechanism to suppress cellular senescence and organismal aging.
source: Hence, these findings not only establish p53 as a substrate for SIRT6, but also identify SIRT6-mediated p53 deacetylation as a critical mechanism to suppress cellular senescence and organismal aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings on the rescue of aging phenotypes.

claim: SIRT6 might target other lysine residues of p53 for deacetylation or other post-translational modifications.
source: Although we have identified lysine 381 of p53 as a major site of deacetylation by SIRT6, we cannot exclude the possibility that SIRT6 might target other lysine residues of p53 for deacetylation or other post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is speculation about potential additional SIRT6 targets on p53.

claim: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice die because of acute aging-associated degenerative processes.
source: Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice have been reported to die because of acute aging-associated degenerative processes, such as severe organ degeneration, body wasting, abruptly lowered serum IGF-1 levels, gut inflammation and chronic metabolic disorders (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication describing causes of death in Sirt6-deficient mice.

claim: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice showed signs of severe body wasting during their terminal lifespan (around 12-16 months).
source: The Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice showed signs of severe body wasting during their terminal lifespan (around 12-16 months).
evidence: This is an observation from the study on late-life phenotypes.

claim: Mixed genetic background has been reported to extend the lifespan of a percentage of Sirt6-deficient mice.
source: Although mixed genetic background has been reported to extend the lifespan of a percentage of Sirt6-deficient mice (Peshti et al., 2017), all the analyses in our study have been done on littermate Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ and Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice (both on mixed backgrounds), where the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice had reduced lifespan of around 4 weeks and the Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice exhibited extended maximal lifespan over the littermate Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This statement cites a publication showing mixed background effects on Sirt6-deficient mice.

claim: The median lifespan for both male and female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice on mixed background is significantly longer than that of the reported Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice on mixed background.
source: Moreover, the median lifespan for both male and female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice on mixed background observed in our study is significantly longer than that of the reported Sirt6-/-Trp53+/+ mice on mixed background (Peshti et al., 2017).
evidence: This compares the study's findings to a previous publication.

claim: The observed lifespan extension of compound mutant mice is attributable largely to Trp53 heterozygosity.
source: This suggests that the observed lifespan extension of compound mutant mice is indeed attributable largely, if not all, to Trp53 heterozygosity.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with mixed background effects.

claim: Peshti et al. (2017) reported gender-specific differences in lifespan extension upon Sirt6 deficiency in mixed genetic background.
source: Moreover, Peshti et al. (2017) reported gender-specific differences in lifespan extension upon Sirt6 deficiency in mixed genetic background.
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication's findings.

claim: The maximal lifespan of the female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was slightly more than the male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice.
source: Although we did observe that the maximal lifespan of the female Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice was slightly more than the male Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice (Figure 2D and E), the differences were not as striking as reported, suggesting further lifespan extension in Sirt6-deficient mice by Trp53 haploinsufficiency reduces the percentage of gender-specific difference in lifespan.
evidence: This is shown by survival curves in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Retinal disorders were prominently observed in Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice.
source: However, retinal disorders were prominently observed in our Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice similar with that reported in Peshti et al. (2017), consistent with a previous report stating that Sirt6 plays critical roles in the maintenance of retinal functions (Silberman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from the study consistent with previous reports.

claim: Sirt6 plays critical roles in the maintenance of retinal functions.
source: However, retinal disorders were prominently observed in our Sirt6-/-Trp53+/- mice similar with that reported in Peshti et al. (2017), consistent with a previous report stating that Sirt6 plays critical roles in the maintenance of retinal functions (Silberman et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement cites a previous publication on SIRT6's role in retinal function.

claim: The very short lifespan of Sirt6 KO mice could result from oversensitivity to p53 activation associated with the genetic backgrounds used.
source: Another possibility cannot be eliminated that the very short lifespan of Sirt6 KO mice could result from oversensitivity to p53 activation associated with the genetic backgrounds used in the respective studies, thus resulting in enhanced cell death even at low DNA damage levels, thereby accelerating aging.
